news.title: Hackers Breach US Air Force Cloud Computing Platform
news.text: Washington DC: Hackers have reportedly gained access to the US Air Force's flagship cloud computing and control platform, marking the latest in a series of cyber intrusions targeting critical US government infrastructure, according to a Reuters exclusive report cited by Fox News on Friday (local time).According to Fox News, the US Air Force has not publicly confirmed the breach. It also remains unclear who was responsible for the intrusion and whether any data was stolen.The reported breach comes amid a series of cyber incidents involving US intelligence and law enforcement agencies, including apparent intrusions affecting the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).On Tuesday (local time), CNN reported that the CIA and ODNI had suffered an apparent cyberattack affecting unclassified information, citing four sources familiar with the matter.According to CNN, the intrusion targeted a system used by the agencies for open-source intelligence analysis. Although the full extent of the breach remained unclear, officials maintained that no classified information had been affected.An ODNI official told CNN that the incident had not disrupted any critical capabilities or classified systems.Open-source intelligence encompasses commercially available information, including social media content, satellite imagery and other online material. While much of this information is publicly accessible, some is obtained through data vendors and can reveal sensitive details, particularly when combined with other datasets.The latest developments also follow an apparent cyberattack targeting the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by federal, state and local law enforcement agencies to access criminal records, outstanding warrants and background-check information.US President Donald Trump appeared to acknowledge the FBI breach during a phone interview with Fox News on November 21."I will say that it's not good--I don't like that," Trump said when asked about the incident, which CNN had earlier reported.According to CNN, the FBI is investigating the intrusion, which marked the second reported breach involving the bureau in recent months.A former FBI official who had led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN that the NCIC was among the most important information-sharing platforms used by law enforcement agencies, raising concerns that hackers could compromise the reliability of information stored in the database, beyond exposing sensitive records.The FBI had also faced a separate cyberattack in September, when a hacking group known as ShinyHunters targeted sensitive personal information belonging to bureau employees through a recruitment website.According to CNN, some FBI employees were left uncertain about whether their personal information had been compromised. A Canadian cybersecurity researcher and author was subsequently arrested and faces charges in connection with the breach.Earlier, in 2023, hackers accessed a computer system used by the FBI's New York field office for investigations into child sexual exploitation. According to CNN, the compromised system included one used to store images related to the Jeffrey Epstein investigation.The series of reported intrusions has raised broader concerns over the security of sensitive information and critical systems maintained by US government agencies.

news.title: Controversial anti-Israel ad showing little girl on bicycle that aired during Saturday Night Live Thanksgiving special is pulled off air by NBC
news.text:
NBC has pulled a controversial anti-Israel commercial from its airwaves after the ad featuring a little American girl saving up for a bicycle sparked a furious backlash during its Saturday Night Live Thanksgiving special.

The network was accused of promoting antisemitism after broadcasting the 30-second commercial, which contrasted the innocent ambitions of an American child with the devastating injuries suffered by a young Palestinian girl in Gaza.

Senior executives at NBC have said they were unaware of the advertisement until after it was broadcast during Wednesday night's primetime special as Americans gathered to celebrate Thanksgiving.

The network will not air the commercial again, and parent company NBCUniversal is set to reassess its advertising approval procedures.

The advertisement, entitled 'Every Three Seconds,' opens with footage of a little girl carrying out household chores throughout the changing seasons in a bid to earn enough money to buy a bicycle.

She is shown mowing grass, clearing fallen leaves and shoveling snow as she works toward purchasing the bike she spotted in a shop window.

'Over a year, she saved $400 for a new bicycle,' a narrator tells viewers.

But the commercial then takes a disturbing turn, cutting to footage of a Palestinian girl standing on crutches amid the rubble in Gaza, with one of her legs missing.

'Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this,' the narrator declares.

The commercial was funded by the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, a pro-Palestinian nonprofit campaigning to end American military assistance to Israel.

Viewers were directed to a campaign website called No More For Israel, which accuses Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians and encourages Americans to lobby members of Congress against further weapons deals.

The decision to broadcast the commercial during one of NBC's holiday specials provoked outrage from Jewish organizations, former government officials and pro-Israel campaigners.

Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt condemned the network in a blistering statement posted on X.

'Broadcasting an ad that blatantly demonizes the Jewish state and makes false claims about the use of American taxpayer dollars during primetime on the eve of a family holiday isn’t just insensitive. It’s indefensible,' Greenblatt wrote.

'Again and again, why do people in positions of authority fail to demonstrate basic decency, let alone respect, for the Jewish community?

'At a moment of escalating antisemitism, there is no rationale to justify fanning the flames with such a twisted narrative.'

David Friedman, who served as US ambassador to Israel during Donald Trump's first administration, also lashed out at the network.

'This is not a public policy commercial,' Friedman told the New York Post.

'It is a carefully orchestrated lie designed to maximize hatred of Jews and Israel. NBC shows terrible judgment – and perhaps worse – in accepting this vile ad.'

Friedman urged viewers to boycott NBC, accusing the commercial's creators of ignoring the atrocities committed by Hamas during the October 7, 2023, terrorist attack on Israel.

Jewish advocacy organization B'nai B'rith International also demanded answers from network executives, opening its lengthy statement: 'Shame on NBC.'

The organization accused the advertisers of exploiting the suffering of a Palestinian child while disregarding the role of Hamas in the conflict and the defensive capabilities financed through American military assistance, including Israel's Iron Dome missile interception system.

'The suffering of innocent civilians is a tragedy. But using a child's pain to spread a twisted, one-sided story that blames the Jewish state, and by extension Jews everywhere, is disgusting,' the organization said.

'NBC owes the public an explanation. How did this ad meet its standards? Who approved it? And what will NBC do to make sure it never happens again?'

American Jewish Committee CEO Ted Deutch, a former Democratic congressman, acknowledged the suffering of Palestinians but argued the commercial presented a distorted account of the conflict.

'The suffering of Palestinian civilians is real and heartbreaking. But using that suffering to demonize Israel while writing Hamas out of the story isn’t an honest debate,' Deutch wrote.

The controversy also prompted threats from viewers to cancel their subscriptions to NBCUniversal's Peacock streaming service, although others defended the advertisement, arguing that criticism of American military assistance to Israel was not inherently antisemitic.

Unlike advertisements purchased by legally qualified political candidates, which broadcasters are generally prohibited from censoring, political issue advertisements funded by outside organizations can be rejected by television stations.

The current American military assistance agreement with Israel was reached under President Barack Obama in 2016 and provides for $38 billion in aid across a decade, covering fiscal years 2019 through 2028.

The Daily Mail has sought comment from NBC, the IMEU Policy Project and the FCC.
news.summary: NBC has pulled a controversial anti-Israel advertisement that aired during its Saturday Night Live Thanksgiving special following a furious backlash.

news.title: Being Born in America Doesn't Make You More American Than Harmeet Dhillon
news.text:
One of those places is blatant racism and bigotry. Too many Republicans online have come to believe that being born in the United States makes them more American than anyone else, including legal immigrants. That belief has fueled a rise in attacks on conservative warriors whose actions and devotion to this country make them more American than the vast majority of people will ever be.

Former Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights at the U.S. Department of Justice, Harmeet Dhillon is one of the people targeted by this racism and bigotry. 

She has always been a bulldog of a conservative attorney. In the Trump administration, she has led more than 100 investigations and settlements involving universities over discriminatory practices and antisemitism. She has brought lawsuits over alleged hiring discrimination, including cases involving H-1B visa preferences and state or local hiring policies, and has worked to protect gun owners' rights. Her record runs even deeper in private practice. She founded the Dhillon Law Group, whose clients have included Donald Trump, his campaigns, and affiliated PACs in free speech, campaign finance, election, and employment disputes. She also founded the Center for American Liberty, a nonprofit that litigates civil liberties cases, including First Amendment and religious freedom cases.

And yet, amid a flurry of right-wing frustration over H-1B visas that has bled into overt racism, primarily against Indians, she has become a target, having been born in India, belonging to the Sikh faith, and being proud of where she comes from, as most of us are. 

A series of accounts claiming to be America First or young conservative groups have launched horrific campaigns, posting things like "Day 1 of trying to get @HarmeetKDhillon to move back to India." Another wrote: "Let's get one thing straight Harmeet. You are not an American. A piece of paper does not make you American and your disdain for real Americans proves that point even further. You should go home and take care of your country. India, that is." Others have called her a demon worshipper and suggested that because she isn't Christian, she is somehow less American.

Yet another attack came from Andrew Branca, a self-described "pro-America, pro-Constitution, pro-Western civilization" conservative podcaster and practicing attorney in a now deleted X post. He asked whether there was "a particular reason WHY [Dhillon] prefer[s] to NOT live in India?" insinuating that India is an inferior place to live, that her culture is something to escape, and that someone of her background can never fully belong in America.

And this isn't even the bulk of it. Attacks like these have become routine against Indian Americans, and even Indians, online. Nearly all of them come from groyper-adjacent, Christian nationalist, and "heritage American" ethnic nationalist voices, emboldened by Republican enthusiasm. 

Dhillon, for her part, has been fighting back, something she couldn't do while serving in the Trump administration.

For our founder and managing partner, Harmeet Dhillon (@HarmeetKDhillon) , the attacks on her background and Sikh faith are nothing new. Growing up, she faced name-calling and prejudice. Those experiences gave her the determination to speak up, even when doing so makes her a target. She understands the pressure to stay silent and the fear that challenging hatred will bring more attacks. She has made a career in part by fighting against the “heckler’s veto”. She knows she isn’t the only person facing these attacks, but she has a public platform, and she intends to use it to defend herself and others.— Dhillon Law Group (@dhillonlaw) November 24, 2026

Let's get one thing clear: any legal immigrant or citizen, foreign- or domestic-born, who loves this country, stands for its principles, and wants to help guide it toward a golden future is just as American as anyone else. Religion, station, and every other immutable characteristic are beside the point. In fact, I would happily say that many legal immigrants are more American than the average American-born Democrat voter.

Dhillon is one such person. If it were up to me, every voice questioning her status as an American would be replaced by a legal immigrant just like her.

news.title: 'Would Agree With Democrats': Republicans Open To Rethinking Trump's Tariffs
news.text: Democrats hoping to blunt President Donald Trump's tariffs when they retake control of Congress may find partners in an unlikely place: among his fellow Republicans.After devastating election losses that centered on rising costs, many Republicans said they're open to reconsidering some of the levies that have become a central plank of Trump's global trade agenda. The administration proposed new tariffs on Wednesday targeting China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.Whether Republicans actually buck Trump on tariffs could signal if election losses and the president's lame duck status shake what has been nearly lockstep fealty to him.In interviews with more than a half dozen congressional Republicans since the election, most said they were open to reviewing tariffs, at least on a case-by-case basis. They expressed a desire for predictability and said Congress could reclaim its constitutional authority over tariffs. They were reluctant, however, to broadly curb the president's own tariff powers and acknowledged Trump could veto any repeal legislation.But for Democrats eager to score some early bipartisan wins, the mere willingness of Republicans to revisit some tariffs could create an opening."A rethink is indeed in order," said Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind. "I'll be a bipartisan voice for making sure we have the most consumer friendly tariff approaches and I think there will be a whole lot of receptivity within the administration to my approach."Rep. Michael Guest, R-Miss., said "there may be some areas that I would agree with the Democrats.""I would personally be opposed to just a blanket restriction on the president's ability to impose tariffs," he said. "But I would be willing to look at it on a case-by-case basis based on what the Democrats may bring forward."Trump has made tariffs a defining feature of his second term, calling himself "Mr. Tariff" as he imposed broad levies on imports from allies and adversaries alike. He insists tariffs will revive American manufacturing and strengthen the US economy, though there is scant evidence they have accomplished those goals. Tariffs often increase costs for consumers in the form of a tax.His aggressive approach marks a sharp departure from the free-trade orthodoxy long embraced by Republicans before Trump moved the party in a more protectionist direction.If Democrats and Republicans were to unite on the issue, tariffs on Canada could emerge as an early test. Previous repeal efforts won support from a handful of Republicans.Democrats, including incoming Senate Finance Committee Chairman Ron Wyden of Oregon, have already identified the Canada tariffs as a top target. And after the levies spurred retribution from Canada, adding to the GOP's election challenges this year, there could be an incentive for more Republicans to join the effort.Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., who is up for reelection in 2028 and was not among the Republicans who backed the Canada repeal legislation, said he distinguished the Canadian tariffs from levies on other countries like China, which he supports."Tariffs with respect to Canada don't make sense to me," he said.Young, who also backs some tariffs on China and faces reelection in 2028, made several social media posts in the days after the election saying voters were "rightly focused on the cost of living." He said one reason for high costs was a tariff structure that is "overly broad, and as a result, it is negatively affecting too many American factory floors, farms, small businesses, and family budgets."In the interview, he said tariffs should be "predictable" and focused on goals such as "reshoring strategic goods or applying leverage on trading partners to liberalize their own markets."When asked about the Canadian levies, he said he was open to different approaches. But he said he preferred that the administration consult with Congress as part of negotiations to renew the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the regional trade pact known as USMCA."The USMCA process seems to work if Congress is actively involved and not patted on the head," he said.Republicans are taking an increasingly assertive posture toward the administration. Since the election, Republicans have expressed skepticism about a sudden $50 billion request for the nation's air travel system after air traffic was briefly shuttered. They've pressed for more details about widespread tech outages and criticized Trump's intervention in returning Jensen Huang to the helm of Nvidia.That bullishness could extend to tariffs."Congress has, over a period of years, recognized that Congress, by itself, has a real difficult time making a tariff and then authorizing and enacting it," said Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota. "So they've given authorities to the executive branch over a period of years. Some of that has cascaded.""There's nothing wrong," he added, "with Congress taking a second look at whether or not those authorities should be withdrawn, modified, at least reconsidered, or limited."Still, reversal of the tariffs is far from guaranteed. For one, Republicans are still sorting through the lessons of this year's elections.Rep. Steve Womack, an Arkansas Republican who said he would consider tariff repeals on a case-by-case basis, said he thought the levies "have played a role in some of the affordability issues.""I have producers in my district that lament the fact that they're paying higher for goods that can't be sourced domestically," he said.But Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., expressed concern the party may overcorrect."I bet a lot of my Republican colleagues will be happy to join Democrats and get rid of a bunch of them, which makes me just a little nervous that it's going to be a dramatic pendulum swing," he said.White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said "this administration is committed to rebuilding the American communities left behind by previous administrations and will continue fighting to lower costs, expand opportunity, and make life more affordable for hardworking American families."Republican voters appeared mixed on the issue.About half of voters who backed the Republican candidate in their local U.S. House race said Trump's tariff policies had helped the national economy, according to The AP Voter Poll. About 3 in 10 said they hurt the U.S. economy, and about one-quarter said those policies didn't make a difference.When it came to their local economy, fewer saw a benefit.About 3 in 10 said Trump's tariff policies helped the economy in their area, and roughly one-quarter said it had hurt it. About 4 in 10 said those policies hadn't impacted the economy in their local area.Democrats, meanwhile, are contemplating a more sweeping challenge to Trump's trade policies.Wyden said that if Democrats were successful in winning Republican support to repeal Canadian tariffs, "we'll have some momentum for going after other tariffs."His counterpart in the House, incoming Ways and Means Committee Chairman Richard Neal, said rescinding tariffs on Canada "might be a good starting point.""But I think taking up the tariffs discussion in totality is really important, largely because the way they've been used in a punitive manner," he said.But no hurdle is as formidable as Trump's veto, which would require support from 67 senators to overturn, a steep challenge even with Democrats poised to enjoy a 56-seat majority.Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., a fervent tariff opponent, said he would back repeals but they would have to be attached to must-pass pieces of legislation for them to have any hope."On its own, he'll just veto it," he said.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: After devastating election losses that centered on rising costs, many Republicans said they're open to reconsidering some of the levies that have become a central plank of Trump's global trade agenda.
news.author: Associated Press

news.title: 'He Did Damage to Individuals': Rudy Giuliani Colleague Goes Off on 'Malevolent' Ex-Mayor After Trump Awards Him Presidential Medal of Freedom
news.text:
Democratic election lawyer Marc Elias criticized former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani after President Donald Trump awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom, RadarOnline.com has learned.

Elias said he had not expected to speak publicly about Giuliani again after opposing the lawsuits brought by Trump's legal team following the 2020 presidential election.Mark Elias Blasts Rudy Giuliani"I thought that that was the last that I'd have to speak about Rudy Giuliani," Elias said in a video posted by Democracy Docket. "I've not found the need to talk about Rudy Giuliani as a figure of the past. But then came this."

Elias argued that Giuliani's recognition was troubling because of his role in efforts to overturn the election.

"But watching Donald Trump shake hands with a man in Rudy Giuliani, who used so much talent that he once had... to try to subvert the outcome of elections and to destroy individual election officials and workers along the way... I couldn't let the moment pass," Elias said.'There was a Darker Side to Rudy Giuliani'Elias recalled initially viewing Giuliani's post-election conduct with bewilderment.

"There was a darker side to Rudy Giuliani that frankly at the time I was not paying that close attention to," Elias said. "Rudy Giuliani, I later came to understand, was running around the country testifying before legislators and frankly defaming election workers."

"He did real damage," Elias continued. "I mean, he did damage to himself. He did damage to democracy. He did damage to the rule of law."

"He did damage to individuals," Elias said. "Individual election workers faced death threats, faced lies, faced all kinds of hate."

Elias rejected the idea that Giuliani's actions could be dismissed as the mistakes of someone whose political career was already declining.

"He was not just a declining old man," Elias noted. "He was not someone just past his prime. He was a malevolent figure. And that's the Rudy Giuliani that history will remember."Rudy Giuliani's Election ClaimsGiuliani was found liable for defaming Georgia election workers Ruby Freeman and her daughter, Wandrea 'Shaye' Moss, after falsely accusing them of manipulating ballots during the 2020 election.

A federal jury awarded the women approximately $148million in damages in December 2023. The judgment was satisfied in February 2025 following a confidential settlement, although the amount Giuliani ultimately paid was not disclosed.

Giuliani was also disbarred in New York and Washington, D.C.

"For that, he wound up living a life of disgrace," Elias said, describing Giuliani as "a disgraced figure that harmed real people."

"I've been clear, like I said, that Rudy Giuliani will be remembered as a coward, as an enabler of Donald Trump, as someone who used his law degree to subvert democracy," Elias added. "So I'm not going easy on him."White House Defends Rudy GiulianiTrump presented Giuliani with the nation's highest civilian honor Tuesday during a private Oval Office ceremony.

White House spokesperson Olivia Wales defended the decision, saying, "Mayor Rudy Giuliani is a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our Nation."

Elias said the ceremony reflected his concerns about the country's political institutions.

"We continue to be in a constitutional crisis because that is the image of what one political party, one political movement believes deserves that high honor."
news.summary: Election lawyer Marc Elias criticized former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani after Trump awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
news.author: Patrick Previty

news.title: France seeks to preserve UNIFIL’s role in Lebanon as withdrawal looms
news.text: Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said Friday that France is drafting a United Nations Security Council resolution that would allow the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) to continue operating after its mandate expires at the end of 2026. Several diplomatic efforts have recently been underway to fill the vacuum, most notably a French-led initiative to deploy an international force of European and U.S. troops. Israel has sought to block the plan, arguing that such a force would allow Hezbollah to operate freely. In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press, Salam said the proposed resolution would allow UNIFIL, established nearly 50 years ago, to continue carrying out some of its duties while the U.N. Security Council considers what should replace it. He also addressed the suspension of negotiations with Israel, saying the talks had been put on hold following Israel’s elections and amid uncertainty over the composition of its next government. Salam said UNIFIL would continue to clear mines, escort humanitarian convoys and monitor violations in southern Lebanon. U.S. officials have indicated that Washington could be “open to considering” such an arrangement, he added. "This would not resolve the problem of so-called post-UNIFIL, but it will give us some extra time to agree on a new architecture in southern Lebanon," Salam added. The AP noted that the Lebanese prime minister’s remarks underscore the fact that there is still no plan for a force to replace UNIFIL, about a month before its mandate is due to expire following opposition from the United States and Israel. Israel has expressed firm opposition to the force’s continued operations, arguing that it has failed in its mission. The administration of President Donald Trump, which has already cut U.S. funding for the force, viewed it as a waste of money and argued that its continued operations were hindering efforts to weaken Hezbollah and transfer full security responsibility in the area to the Lebanese army. Israeli criticism of UNIFIL’s performance also emerged during a visit by a ynet reporter to the ruins of the “Hezbollah tents” compound on Mount Dov. Reserve Lt. Col. Y., commander of the 221st Battalion, told the reporter that maps marking IDF positions had been discovered in outposts vacated by UNIFIL. "This tank position, another tank position and the deployment of our outposts," he said. "We enter one of these UNIFIL outposts, near the IDF's Balut outpost, and find maps and markings of Israeli military positions posted on its windows." "The astonishing thing about UNIFIL is that they stood here along the border, watching and monitoring us — as if we were the enemy," Lt. Col. Y. added. "You suddenly realize that their watchtowers are facing us. Their mandate is to ensure that Hezbollah does not deploy ammunition south of the Litani River and that we do not cross the border. In practice, we did not cross, while Hezbollah moved vast quantities of weapons into the area for 18 years following the Second Lebanon War. All the roads you see crisscrossing this area were paved by the U.N. and used by Hezbollah." Under a U.N. Security Council resolution adopted last year, the roughly 7,500 UNIFIL troops deployed in southern Lebanon are to withdraw gradually over a six-month period after the force’s mandate expires on Dec. 31, 2026. The resolution also gives UNIFIL a year to wind down its operations entirely. France has not commented on the proposal to extend the force’s operations. However, a Western diplomat with knowledge of the matter said one option under discussion is to slow down the withdrawal process and “maintain certain UNIFIL missions” to avoid a power vacuum. The diplomat spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the matter. During diplomatic talks over what would follow UNIFIL’s withdrawal, France pushed for the deployment of an international force comprising several thousand French, Italian and Spanish troops. The force would operate not only in southern Lebanon but throughout the country, helping the Lebanese army establish control over its territory. Israel opposed the proposal. "After all, they haven't fired a single shot at Hezbollah," an Israeli official previously remarked. France put forward another proposal under which the Security Council would issue a new mandate to establish a force of several hundred observers from European countries to monitor developments in Lebanon, with an emphasis on the south of the country and designated pilot areas. Israel also opposed this proposal, viewing it as a form of “UNIFIL 2.0” that would be unable to fulfill its mission. Israel also feared that protecting the force would require several thousand additional troops. Meanwhile, the United States explored the possibility of establishing a smaller, 100-member observer force made up of troops from the United States and several other countries to monitor the implementation of security arrangements in designated pilot areas.
news.summary: With UNIFIL’s 7,500 troops due to begin withdrawing in about a month, France is drafting a proposal to retain some of its missions and prevent a security vacuum in southern Lebanon amid fierce Israeli opposition and uncertainty over a replacement force
news.author: Lior Ben Ari

news.title: Starshield restrictions cause heavy Ukrainian drone losses, canceled operations — report
news.text:
MOSCOW, November 28. /TASS/. Restrictions on the Starshield satellite communication system used by the Ukrainian armed forces have led to heavy drone losses and the cancellation of a number of operations, The Kyiv Independent reported, citing high-ranking Ukrainian military officials.

Specifically, one Ukrainian military source told the publication that the restrictions significantly affected FP-2 medium-range strike drones. According to the source, limitations on Starshield’s operation resulted in "extremely high drone losses" during certain operations, while others had to be called off entirely.

Another senior Ukrainian military official called the move to restrict the Starshield system a "political decision."

Earlier, Vladimir Zelensky said the Ukrainian armed forces had also faced difficulties intercepting drones due to ongoing issues with access to Starshield. In mid-November, Zelensky claimed that the Ukrainian armed forces’ access to Starshield had been restricted for five days. In October, Kiev also complained about speed limitations when using Starshield. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump said he was unaware of any restrictions on access to the Starlink satellite communication system in Ukraine.
news.summary: In a conversation with The Kyiv Independent, a senior Ukrainian military official called the move a "political decision"
news.author: Tass

news.title: Katie Miller Quietly Scrubs Swipe at Unlikely Media Target
news.text:
As footage of the White House appeared on screen, Michaels remarked: “Looking back at the White House, always beautiful to see the White House regardless of the resident of that home.” 

The innocuous comment was not neutral enough for MAGA’s online warriors, who took it as a slight against President Donald Trump.

“Legacy media can’t even do the weather without bias,” Miller fumed in the now-deleted post. 

The post went up just after 9 p.m. on Thursday, but had vanished by early Friday morning, when it was highlighted by the Bad Fox Graphics X account. 

Miller, who is married to Trump’s chief of staff, Stephen Miller, 41, wasn’t the only outraged member of the MAGA tribe. 

Conservative radio host Mike Opelka helped fuel the backlash, posting the clip with the caption: “Hey, @weatherchannel - wut??? ‘the White House, always beautiful, regardless of the resident of that home.’”

His replies were filled with MAGA supporters vowing to boycott the Weather Channel.

Some claimed they were deleting the Weather Channel app over the remark, while others called for Michaels to be fired. 

In a reply to one of his critics, Michaels defended his words.

“In such a polarized society, it’s a completely legitimate thing to say. I don’t care who lives in that house. It’s gorgeous. And we’re lucky to have it,” he wrote.

The furor continued Friday morning, even after Miller had deleted her post, with pro-Trump influencer Juanita Broaddrick joining the calls for Michaels to be canned.

“Is this A-hole, Justin Michaels, still employed at The Weather Channel @weatherchannel ??? This is just unbelievable!! 😡" she wrote to her two million followers. 

Miller did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and she has not publicly explained why she deleted the post. 

Miller has made a habit of scrubbing controversial posts. In October, she removed a “Promise made, promise kept” message celebrating a federal search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home.

Just last week, she deleted a screenshot of Trump’s threat to Iran that “a whole civilization will die tonight” about an hour after sharing it.
news.summary:
MANDEL NGAN / AFP via Getty ImagesMAGA maven Katie Miller aimed her outrage at a Weather Channel reporter in a social media post late on Thanksgiving before quietly deleting it. 

Miller, 35, took umbrage at a comment by the Weather Channel’s Justin Michaels, 47, a national correspondent covering the nor’easter from Washington, D.C., on Thanksgiving Day.

Read more at The Daily Beast.
news.author: Sarah-Jane Collins

news.title: Trump Torched by Critics After Declaring Israel's Military Has Been 'Decimated' in Wild Rant
news.text:
Donald Trump is facing criticism after appearing to confuse Israel with Iran during a press exchange about Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Israel's incoming leadership, RadarOnline.com can report.

Asked how he was preparing to deal with Israel’s next leadership, the president described a military that had been “decimated,” with its air force, navy and anti-aircraft defenses "wiped out."Apparent Mix-Up on Israel’s LeadershipAlthough he did not name the country, his subsequent references to nuclear sites and Pickaxe Mountain appeared to indicate he was discussing Iran.

Trump was taking questions at Mar-a-Lago on Thanksgiving, November 26, when a reporter asked whether he planned to speak with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"Have you had a chance at all this week or in the coming days do you plan to speak with Prime Minister Netanyahu," the reporter asked.

"I have," Trump replied.

The reporter then followed up, "And how are you preparing to deal with the next incoming Israeli leadership?"

The 80-year-old responded, "Well, you know, we're trying to give them a chance to be smart. They, they have no military," before describing the military as decimated.

"Their military is decimated. Their air force is wiped out. Their navy is wiped out. Their anti-aircraft is wiped out," he said. Trump did not identify the country he was referring to or clarify his remarks. 

However, the description appeared to concern Iran rather than Israel.Critics Go Off: He's a 'National Security Threat'Users mocked the president for his gaffe, suggesting he was either too old or incompetent to be discussing foreign affairs. 

Others took the opportunity to compare Trump's demeanor with that of former President Joe Biden, who also faced criticism for his verbal gaffes and fueled speculation about his cognitive health.

"Demented Hitler is a national security threat," one user wrote.

"He isn’t confused. He has no idea what he’s talking about!" another suggested.

"We all know what the reaction would be if this were Pres. Biden. It would be played 24/7 on Fox News with calls for the 25th," a user raged.

"For the umpteenth time today, if Biden did that, Trumpers would be calling for his immediate removal under the 25th Amendment of the Constitution. It’s time to remove Trump. If his flunkies won’t do it under the 25th, let’s just expose the Epstein files and the crimes will do it," a person pointed out.Trump Threatened to Strike Iran’s Pickaxe MountainTrump continued discussing the country's military capabilities and referred to nuclear sites that the U.S. had targeted.

"Now I'm sure they have a little extra; we follow them very closely. They haven't been able to do anything with their nuclear sites that we wiped out. But if we did anything, we would hit Pickaxe. I mean, we can tell them because they can't do anything about it. We would absolutely hit Pickaxe Mountain, but we haven't seen any real activity there,” he said.

The references to nuclear sites and Pickaxe Mountain further suggested Trump was discussing Iran. 

He did not return to the reporter's question about Israel's incoming leadership or explain the apparent discrepancy.Trump Shifts to GDP FiguresTrump later turned to the economy and criticized the Commerce Department after the Bureau of Economic Analysis revised its estimate of third-quarter economic growth to 4.3 percent, up from its earlier estimate of 3.4 percent.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis said the upward revision primarily reflected higher estimates for investment and consumer spending. 

The agency regularly updates GDP estimates as additional information becomes available.

Trump had also criticized the figures in a Thanksgiving Day Truth Social post, demanding an investigation into why what he called the "correct number" had not been released before the election.

Trump had also discussed military production with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte during a meeting at Mar-a-Lago the previous day, declaring, "There has never been a time when the United States has produced more Military Equipment or Munitions than now."
news.summary: Donald Trump is facing criticism after declaring that Israel's military has been 'decimated' during a controversial rant.
news.author: Christian Spencer

news.text:

news.title: EXCLUSIVE: Donald Trump's Vodka Deal at Center of Alleged Double-Cross as Businessmen Accused of Stealing Lucrative Contract
news.text:
President Donald Trump's vodka licensing deal is at the center of a legal battle after two businessmen were accused of posing as investors to obtain confidential information before allegedly securing the lucrative contract for themselves, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

According to court documents obtained by Radar, federal Judge Jorge L. Alonso denied motions to dismiss a lawsuit brought by 45 Spirits LLC and its co-founders, Richard DeCicco and Timothy Klintworth, allowing their legal fight against Zohair Sultan, Sameet Patel, and several affiliated companies to proceed in Illinois.Trump's Vodka Venture Sparks Legal WarDeCicco and Klintworth founded 45 Spirits in May 2023 in anticipation of securing a licensing agreement with the Trump Organization to sell Trump-branded vodka.

By May 2025, the businessmen had reportedly raised enough money to cover the licensing fee and begin operations. However, their plans were allegedly derailed by two prospective investors who expressed interest in committing millions to the venture.

According to the filing, Klintworth first contacted Sultan in December 2024 about an investment opportunity. Sultan subsequently introduced him to Patel through a group text message.

During a conference call, Klintworth allegedly shared detailed documents and confidential information about the company's business plans after receiving verbal assurances that the information would remain private.Millions in Promised InvestmentsOn May 13, 2025, Sultan reportedly told Klintworth he was interested in investing "a couple million" in the company but needed additional time to access the funds.

Klintworth delayed finalizing the Trump Organization deal, believing the additional investment would benefit the business.

Over the following weeks, Sultan allegedly continued requesting confidential information while assuring Klintworth that he and Patel had assembled a group of investors willing to commit several million dollars.

Meanwhile, Patel established a competing company, 47 Spirits, on May 20.Businessmen Blindsided by Rival DealOn June 4, the Trump Organization informed Klintworth it would instead award the licensing agreement to Patel's company.

The plaintiffs allege Sultan and Patel conspired to obtain their confidential information and secure the business opportunity for themselves.

In his November 18 ruling, Alonso outlined allegations that Sultan had "lulled Klintworth into delaying the finalization of the licensing deal" to give Patel time to establish his competing business.

The lawsuit includes claims of trade secret misappropriation, copyright infringement, fraud, breach of contract, and interference with a prospective business relationship.Judge Refuses to Toss LawsuitThe defendants also argued the lawsuit should be dismissed because the Trump Organization had not been named as a defendant.

However, Alonso rejected that argument, explaining the dispute concerns damages allegedly caused by the defendants rather than Trump's company.

"As alleged, there are no damages attributable to the Trump Organization," the judge wrote.

Neither Trump nor the Trump Organization is named as a defendant.

The judge ordered the parties to submit a joint status report by November 25 outlining the next steps in the litigation.

The ruling allows the lawsuit to proceed in Illinois but does not establish whether fraud or trade secret theft occurred.
news.summary: Donald Trump's vodka licensing deal is at the center of a legal battle after businessmen were accused of stealing confidential information to secure the contract.
news.author: Ashlyn Walker

news.title: GOP lawmaker warns Trump's high-stakes rescue will 'come back to bite us in the butt'
news.text:
A GOP lawmaker warned that President Donald Trump's latest decision puts profits ahead of national security and will hurt the U.S. down the line.

During a Friday interview on CNN, Rep. Mark Alford (R-MO) said that he would have liked to see questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang answered before the company reinstated him despite administration assurances that he posed no security threat.

Huang is set to appear on Capitol Hill next week for bipartisan hearings over national security concerns amid reports of his affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as reports that the company's most sensitive chips had found their way to China.

Alford said he "certainly would" have wanted questions about Huang's affair resolved before the president made a move to bring him back as Nvidia CEO.

"I think our national security comes before any stock price or any profit to be made," Alford said.

Earlier in the interview, he chalked up Trump's mixed messages on vetoing Democratic legislation as "President Trump's classic way of basically saying the same thing in several different ways," and stressed that the deal to reinstate Huang wasn't his to make.

"I would have liked to have waited," Alford said. "I'm not the president of the United States. I didn't make the deal to get him reinstated. But the truth must come out."

news.title: Greg Abbott Proves Gina Hinojosa Right With Latest Texas Data Center Move
news.text: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s pause on environmental permits for data center projects ended less than two weeks after he lost reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who had predicted he would lift it after the election. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) had resumed issuing permits by November 16, after Abbott’s office told the agency that the state’s grid operator had finished gathering information on potential impacts on nearby communities. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa had said for months that this would happen. "Greg Abbott invited data centers into Texas when he signed into law House Bill 2712 in 2015 to give hyperscale data centers 20-year tax breaks," her campaign website reads. "A temporary moratorium is a scam because Abbott will likely lift it on November 4th, right after the election. The only way Texans are protected is when real laws are passed." Abbott's office sent its notice to the TCEQ on November 13, 10 days after the election and nine days after the date Hinojosa had predicted. Newsweek reached out to Abbott's office and Hinojosa's transition team for comment via email on Friday. What Abbott Did Abbott signed House Bill 2712 in 2015, creating a 20-year sales and use tax exemption on eligible purchases for qualifying large data center projects. Last November, at an event with Google executives announcing a $40 billion investment in the state, he called Texas the "epicenter of AI development." His tone shifted this summer, as rural communities pushed back against projects that critics said could strain the power grid and local water supplies. At a June 30 campaign stop in Bullard, Abbott called for prohibiting AI data centers in rural Texas neighborhoods and said, "We must eliminate the tax break they are getting." In August, Abbott asked the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) and state electricity regulators to audit every data center seeking a grid connection, looking at tax incentives, power and water use and neighborhood impacts. He paused approvals to power up new large data centers. On September 21, he went further and wrote to the TCEQ, which handles air pollution permits for facilities and stormwater permits for construction sites. "Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects," Abbott said in announcing the directive, referring to the reviews by ERCOT and the Texas Water Development Board. The pause leaked. In October, the advocacy groups Public Citizen and FracTracker Alliance found that some data center construction permits had cleared through the agency's automated filing system despite the order. The TCEQ then suspended 17 construction approvals, shut the electronic system down and required paper applications for staff review. On November 5, two days after the election, ERCOT told the Public Utility Commission it had received responses from 433 of 465 loads, or 93 percent. ERCOT is aiming to publish its full findings on December 10, and regulators plan to discuss them at a December 17 meeting. The permits started moving anyway. TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said the agency "has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations." One of the first approvals after the freeze was an air permit for a gas-fired power plant serving SpaceX’s proposed $24 billion data center project at Starbase in the Rio Grande Valley, according to Politico. The project includes a dedicated gas-fired power plant with 35 turbines producing about 750 megawatts. Kathryn Guerra of Public Citizen said TCEQ leadership had "begun unilaterally issuing data center permits" without sharing ERCOT's results, and the group called on the agency's commissioners to resign. Sam Law of FracTracker Alliance called for "a true moratorium on data center development." Wall Street noticed too. Analysts at the investment firm TD Cowen wrote that "Abbott's lame-duck-permitting push" would likely harden demands from Democrats that Hinojosa take a firm stand, lowering the odds of a near-term deal between her and developers. What Hinojosa Says She Will Do Hinojosa's campaign called for an immediate moratorium on new data center approvals, lasting "until the legislature can meet to put in place real protections," and a special session to repeal what her website calls "giant tax giveaways." In one campaign video, she burned a copy of the tax break law. At a July press conference, she said data centers were "guzzling up all our water, guzzling up all our electricity" while residents had no say. "That is the Wild West of data centers that Greg Abbott has created in Texas," she said. Speaking to KTAB News before the election, she said her moratorium would apply to "any new permits." "I would have a moratorium or ban in place until we pass those laws that protect Texans and give them a seat at the table again to decide if and how data centers come into their communities," she said. The legislation she wants would require licensed union labor on projects, bar nondisclosure agreements, make developers show households won't pay more for power or water, end subsidies and give communities a voice on where facilities go. Since winning, she has worked to reassure business. "It is not that I hate data centers. I hate the way they are taking advantage of Texas, and that stops when I'm governor," she told CNN. She told Houston's ABC13 that Texas has "always been a pro-business state," but that "what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans." On Fox News, she told Bret Baier she looked forward to working with Elon Musk as long as it benefited Texans. Musk spent about $224 million on Texas political efforts this cycle, including about $212 million backing Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, according to The New York Times. The calendar works against her in the short term. The Legislature convenes January 12, and Hinojosa takes office January 19. Bills passed this spring generally would not take effect until September 1, 2027. She will have some tools on day one. As governor, she can rescind or replace Abbott's directives and designate the chairs of the utility commission and the TCEQ and nominate commissioners as seats become available, subject to Senate confirmation. And repealing the data center sales tax exemption already has support in both parties: Republican Senator Joan Huffman, who chairs the Senate Finance Committee, is one of 23 senators backing the repeal bill. A National Backlash Texas was one front in a fight that spread across the country this year. Critics have pointed to rising power bills, noise, water use and pollution from new gas generators, often for facilities that employ relatively few people once built. New York Governor Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, issued the nation's first statewide moratorium on new hyperscale data centers in July, and lawmakers in more than a dozen other states weighed similar limits. On November 3, voters in 10 states decided 41 local ballot measures on data centers. In 40 of those votes, the outcome favored restrictions or opposed development, according to Ballotpedia. Harwood, North Dakota, was the sole pro-development result in that tally. An NBC exit poll found 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers were a "crucial or major factor" in their vote for Congress. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor's race after campaigning for a statewide pause. The polling had pointed that way for months. A Gallup survey in March found 7 in 10 Americans opposed building an AI data center in their area. Republicans Split, Trump Mocked Critics The opposition cut into the Republican base. An Economist/YouGov poll from August found 47 percent of 2024 Trump voters opposed a new data center in their community, compared with 35 percent who supported one. Several Republicans broke with the White House. Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers called for a one-year statewide moratorium on new construction. President Donald Trump went the other direction. "Communities that don't take a data center, they're making a mistake," he said in an August 21 interview with his former lawyer Michael Cohen. Trump also told reporters that, "If a Republican's against the data center, that's OK with me." On August 31, he posted on Truth Social: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor." He warned against killing the "Golden Goose" and added: "China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement." Tennessee Republican Representative Tim Burchett answered with a line of his own. "I guess I'm backwards and poor," he told MeidasTouch. Vice President JD Vance tried to clarify the post, telling reporters that most of the backlash had come in places where a data center meant higher utility bills. Weeks later he changed his pitch, suggesting companies pay communities a "dividend" to make their projects popular. Political scientist Cal Jillson told Newsweek the shift was unlikely to move voters before November. In Texas, the window between the resumption of environmental permitting and Hinojosa’s inauguration is about two months. ERCOT is aiming to publish its full report December 10. Hinojosa takes the oath on January 19. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Rhian Morgan.
news.summary: Texas resumed issuing data center permits less than two weeks after Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott.

news.title: Son of Hamas chief 'survives Israeli strike' | Dunya News
news.text:
CAIRO (Reuters) - The son of Hamas chief Khalil al-Hayya survived an assassination attempt by the Israeli military on Friday, senior Hamas official Basem Naim said.

He told Reuters that ​Izzeldeen al-Hayya and his family had survived a dawn airstrike and Hamas sources said several people, ‌including Hayya's daughter-in-law, had been wounded but there had been no deaths.

The Israeli military had no immediate comment.

Naim described Izzeldeen al-Hayya, born in 1997, as the Hamas chief's last surviving son, with four others having been killed by Israeli forces. The family of one of the ​late sons survived Friday's strike, Naim said.

Hamas said in a statement that the Israeli military had targeted a ​residential apartment, and linked the attack to threats Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has made ⁠against Hayya.

Hamas accused Israel of seeking to undermine a 2025 Gaza ceasefire agreement and said Israel bore full responsibility ​for the consequences of its continued attacks.

Izzeldeen is the twin brother of Hamam Khalil al-Hayya, who was killed in a ​2025 Israeli airstrike targeting Hamas leaders in Qatar, Naim said.

Named Hamas' overall leader in July, Hayya narrowly escaped assassination himself in the Qatar strike. He warned of possible retaliation on Thursday after Israeli attacks killed at least 10 people in Gaza.

Two separate Israeli strikes killed five Palestinians in ​Gaza on Friday, medics said. The first strike killed three Palestinians and wounded two in the city of Rafah, medical sources ​told Reuters. The Israeli military spokesperson said the military had struck three militants without giving further information.

In the second attack, Palestinian medics ‌said ⁠the two people, who worked as civil guards at an office of the Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) in Gaza City, were killed. There has been no immediate comments by the Israeli military nor by MSF and Reuters couldn’t immediately authenticate whether the two worked for MSF.

Israel has continued to carry out attacks it says target Hamas but the attacks have also killed ​many civilians. The broader ceasefire ​plan, backed by US ⁠President Donald Trump, has not halted the violence or secured Hamas' disarmament.

At least 1,600 Palestinians and 5 Israeli soldiers have been killed since the ceasefire was agreed in October 2025, ​according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies.

Israeli troops control around two-thirds of Gaza, up ​from more than ⁠half at the time of the ceasefire, while Hamas controls a thin piece of territory along Gaza's coast.

Israel's assault on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since 2023, caused a hunger crisis, internally displaced Gaza's entire population and led to assessments ⁠of genocide ​from scholars and a United Nations inquiry.

Israel has denied the allegations ​of genocide, saying it acted in self-defence after Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took more than 250 hostages in an attack on Israel in ​October 2023.

news.title: Iraq oil smuggling clampdown threatens ties with Kurds, Iran
news.text:
BAGHDAD: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi is taking bold steps to curb rampant oil smuggling, moves that the US has praised but that risk putting him at odds with Iraq’s Kurds and neighboring Iran.

Iraq has long been stuck balancing the competing influence of the United States and Iran. But Zaidi has been steering the country closer to Washington and has been lauded by President Donald Trump.

On Friday, Trump said he backs Zaidi’s “efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state.”

Zaidi, who has repeatedly vowed to disarm Iran-backed armed groups, recently went after a powerful faction over alleged oil smuggling.

On Tuesday, he also moved to place the Kurdistan region’s border crossings and several oil fields under federal control — a step that would tighten Baghdad’s grip on the autonomous region while cutting smuggling routes into Iran.

US interests 

Zaidi enjoys close ties with Trump envoy Tom Barrack, who is driving efforts to expand US oil investments in Iraq and develop an export route through Syria that could reduce the dependence on the Strait of Hormuz.

Yet the US must first deal with two main challenges: Iran-backed groups hostile to its interests, and rampant smuggling that gives a lifeline to Iran and threatens investments.

The US, which is intensifying its economic pressure against the Islamic republic, accuses Tehran of using Iraq to evade sanctions, and has previously sanctioned Iraqi individuals and companies for blending Iraqi and Iranian oil.

Sajad Jiyad, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said that Zaidi’s “strategy is aligned with what America wants for Iraq and for its Iran policy.”

“A stronger central government serves US interests better,” as it can better control the country and rein in armed groups, even if that weakens traditional US allies such as the Kurdistan authorities, the Baghdad-based analyst said.

Zaidi’s crackdown on oil smuggling through Kurdistan targets routes used to move crude into Iran where it is being blended with Iranian crude for export, according to an intelligence document cited by Iraq’s state media.

Cutting off that flow is “exactly what US policy is right now: maximum pressure through economic blockade,” Jiyad said.

Earlier this month, Zaidi went after Kataeb Hezbollah, a powerful Iran-backed group that refuses to give up its weapons, over alleged oil smuggling in its stronghold south of Baghdad.

He later sent government forces into the area under a compromise deal that averted a confrontation.

Several Iraqi political sources told AFP that Zaidi’s relationship with Tehran has strained and that Iran will not accept that its allied factions disarm amid a regional war.

Zaidi’s decision to put Kurdistan’s border crossings and several oil fields under federal control sparked angry reactions from Kurdish authorities.

Relations between Baghdad and Irbil, the capital of Kurdistan, have long been tense, with recurring disputes over territories, oil exports or budget allocations.

Iraq’s Kurds, who have close ties with the US, have repeatedly warned of federal government attempts to undermine their autonomy, which was formalized by Iraq’s 2005 constitution.

They have become more wary recently seeing that US policy in Syria has denied the Kurds there autonomy in favor of centralized authority in Damascus.

Irbil-based political analyst Lawk Ghafuri said that the Kurds will consider Zaidi’s decision a “threat,” but they will eventually strike a deal, adding that Zaidi’s strategy is to rise the stakes enough to secure concessions.

Judiciary chief Faeq Zaidan, widely seen as close to Zaidi, has called for a dialogue next week to diffuse tensions.

At its core, Zaidi’s goal is to rein in armed groups, assert greater control over oil wealth and draw foreign investment, Ghafuri said.

Financial relief 

The Middle East war and the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz dealt a blow to Iraq’s oil exports, which make up 90 percent of its revenues.

The US has also slowed cash shipments for Iraq’s oil sales, handled by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York since 2003.

Government spokesperson Haidar Al-Aboudi told state media that Iraq’s losses due to oil smuggling from Kurdistan exceeded $100 billion between 2008 to 2025.

Kurdish authorities used to export oil independently, without the approval of the federal government, which has consistently insisted that all oil exports fall under its authority.

Jiyad said Iraq is facing a big deficit, and Zaidi is also “trying to find ways to increase public revenues and one of those is to stop” losing money to oil smuggling.
news.summary: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi's crackdown on oil smuggling is garnering praise from the US but risks straining relations with Iraq's Kurds and Iran. By aiming to centralize control over oil resources and border crossings, Zaidi seeks to assert state authority and combat corruption, which the US supports in its effort to counter Iran's influence and secure investments in Iraq. However, this move has sparked tensions with Kurdish authorities, who fear a threat to their autonomy.

news.title: 'The Real Fraud': MAGA Trump Impersonator Shawn Farash Torched by Critics After Marjorie Taylor Greene Exposes Thanksgiving Photo Claim
news.text:
MAGA Trump impersonator Shawn Farash is facing backlash from both sides of the aisle after Marjorie Taylor Greene exposed his claim that her Thanksgiving photo was recycled from last year, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

The comedian, known for his viral Donald Trump impression, accused the former congresswoman of faking her holiday post. Greene responded with receipts that proved otherwise.Shawn Farash Claims MTG Photo Is OldThe controversy began Thursday evening when Farash posted on X that Greene's Thanksgiving photo was not from this year. He pointed to a football game visible on a television in the background.

"Marjorie Taylor Greene is such a fraud...The Redskins did not play today. This is last year's game," Farash wrote, claiming the broadcast did not match the 2026 Thanksgiving NFL schedule.

"This picture isn't even from this year. Wonder what she's hiding?" he added. The post spread quickly, amplified by several prominent pro-Trump accounts.MTG Fires Back With Metadata ReceiptsGreene, who has split publicly with Trump since leaving Congress, fired back within hours with direct evidence.

She posted the metadata from her iPhone showing the photo was taken at 6:14 p.m. on November 26, 2026, along with a second image snapped seconds later showing a different scene on the television.

"Here is the meta data details of my Thanksgiving photo from yesterday. I did not post an old photo from last year," Greene wrote.

In the same post, she wrote, "You do realize during football games, they show NFL promotions and commercials, right? The real FRAUD is Shawn Farash and anyone spreading this outright petty and pathetic attempt to discredit and smear me."Shaw Farash Admits He Was WrongOn November 27, Farash publicly retracted his claim after reviewing Greene's metadata evidence.

"After reviewing the play, and in light of the Metadata that was posted, the photo appears to not be an old photo. I'll own it. I thought it was from last year. I got this one wrong," he wrote.

He added, "My bad Marge," but included a swipe at Greene over her recent criticism of the Army's plan to demolish a degraded explosives stockpile in Iowa.

The admission came after Greene's rebuttal drew criticism of Farash from MAGA supporters who had initially amplified his theory.Critics Torch Impersonator OnlineThe fallout did not end with the retraction. Greene's label stuck as critics continued to hammer Farash online, echoing her claim that he was the real fraud and questioning his credibility as a MAGA commentator.

"The worst part of this isn’t that you got owned so hard, it’s that it was an effort for something so incredibly childish and pathetic," one person raged on X.

Another said, "You must live a very boring life, buddy," while a third commentator noted, "Too late. You’re a proven fraud and a complete a-shole.

The episode sparked a second claim from another pro-Trump account that circled a clock on a shelf behind Greene, arguing the time did not match the metadata. Greene responded that the clock was not working.

Greene later wrote, "MAGA is so stupid now, it's beyond repair," after facing two challenges to her Thanksgiving photos in less than a day.

Farash, who performs as Captain Deplorable and has built a large following on TikTok and X for his Trump impression, has not deleted his original posts.
news.summary: The controversy started when Shawn Farash posted on X that Marjorie Taylor Greene's Thanksgiving photo was not from this year.

news.title: Hackers reportedly breach US Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform
news.text:
Hackers have reportedly gained access to the US Air Force's flagship cloud computing and control platform, marking the latest in a series of cyber intrusions targeting critical US government infrastructure, according to a Reuters exclusive report cited by Fox News on Friday, said ANI.

According to Fox News, the US Air Force has not publicly confirmed the breach. It also remains unclear who was responsible for the intrusion and whether any data was stolen.

The reported breach comes amid a series of cyber incidents involving US intelligence and law enforcement agencies, including apparent intrusions affecting the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

On Tuesday (local time), CNN reported that the CIA and ODNI had suffered an apparent cyberattack affecting unclassified information, citing four sources familiar with the matter.

According to CNN, the intrusion targeted a system used by the agencies for open-source intelligence analysis. Although the full extent of the breach remained unclear, officials maintained that no classified information had been affected.

An ODNI official told CNN that the incident had not disrupted any critical capabilities or classified systems.

Open-source intelligence encompasses commercially available information, including social media content, satellite imagery and other online material. While much of this information is publicly accessible, some is obtained through data vendors and can reveal sensitive details, particularly when combined with other datasets.

The latest developments also follow an apparent cyberattack targeting the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by federal, state and local law enforcement agencies to access criminal records, outstanding warrants and background-check information.

US President Donald Trump appeared to acknowledge the FBI breach during a phone interview with Fox News on November 21.

"I will say that it's not good--I don't like that," Trump said when asked about the incident, which CNN had earlier reported.

According to CNN, the FBI is investigating the intrusion, which marked the second reported breach involving the bureau in recent months.

A former FBI official who had led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN that the NCIC was among the most important information-sharing platforms used by law enforcement agencies, raising concerns that hackers could compromise the reliability of information stored in the database, beyond exposing sensitive records.

The FBI had also faced a separate cyberattack in September, when a hacking group known as ShinyHunters targeted sensitive personal information belonging to bureau employees through a recruitment website.

According to CNN, some FBI employees were left uncertain about whether their personal information had been compromised. A Canadian cybersecurity researcher and author was subsequently arrested and faces charges in connection with the breach.

Earlier, in 2023, hackers accessed a computer system used by the FBI's New York field office for investigations into child sexual exploitation. According to CNN, the compromised system included one used to store images related to the Jeffrey Epstein investigation.

The series of reported intrusions has raised broader concerns over the security of sensitive information and critical systems maintained by US government agencies.

news.title: Ted Cruz Blames China for Data Center Water Fears: 'You're Being Lied To'
news.text: Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas said Friday that China is funding influence campaigns to convince Americans that artificial intelligence data centers consume excessive amounts of water, calling such concerns "false" and part of a broader effort to slow the nation's technological development. Speaking on his Verdict podcast with political commentator Ben Ferguson, Cruz alleged that China-backed operations have rapidly shifted public opinion against data centers to gain an advantage in the global race for AI dominance. "If you're worried data centers are stealing your water, you're being lied to. That is a false argument," Cruz said. "China is paying money to convince you [that] you should be scared." Newsweek reached out to Cruz's office and the Chinese Embassy for comment by email. The Battle Over AI Infrastructure Texas has become a central battleground over AI infrastructure due to its available land, energy resources and business-friendly regulatory climate. State officials and technology firms have promoted the multibillion-dollar investments as vital to economic growth and national competitiveness. The Lone Star State is one of the nation's largest and fastest-growing data center markets, with more than 400 facilities operating statewide as of September 2025, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). The research organization estimates that existing Texas data centers consume about 25 billion gallons of water annually for direct cooling and electricity generation, a figure projected to rise as AI development accelerates. At the same time, disputes over water demand, electricity consumption, local control and environmental impacts have grown increasingly prominent in state politics. Kathryn Guerra, the Dallas-based campaign director for Public Citizen's TCEQ Watchdog program, told Newsweek that Cruz is out of touch with what's happening in Texas communities. "Gaslighting Texans about water concerns isn’t going to help, but what could have helped is transparency around water consumption–something state leadership failed to ensure," she said. "Texans deserve clear answers about how much water data centers will consume, their water source and how regulators will enforce limits. Until companies are compelled to report water data with real penalties for non-compliance, Texans will remain unconvinced." Cruz Alleges Foreign Interference Cruz said on Friday that China views AI as a strategic competition with the United States and benefits when Americans oppose data center construction. "China and America are in a race for AI," he said. "If you're [Chinese President] Xi [Jinping] in China, the single best way to win this race is convince America handcuff themselves, tie their hands, stop developing AI, surrender, and let China win," the senator said. According to Ferguson, foreign influence campaigns have played a major role in turning the public against the facilities, particularly by amplifying concerns over water usage. "We've found out not that long ago that there [were] hundreds of thousands of bots that were basically putting misinformation, scare tactics in the marketplace to turn people away from data centers," he said. "That was all, by the way, being paid for by China." Cruz added: "The number one and number two argument against data centers: number one, water. You need to understand if you're worried data centers are stealing your water, you're being lied to." He maintained that newer facilities increasingly rely on closed-loop or air-cooling systems that require minimal water. "Almost every data center going in uses either what's called closed-loop cooling, which means the same water gets circulated round and round and round, so it uses almost no water," Cruz said. "So almost every data center uses less water than a golf course." Who Is Winning the AI Race? Most analysts continue to view the United States as the overall leader in frontier AI development. American companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and Meta operate many of the world's most advanced AI models and attract the largest private-sector investment. President Donald Trump has repeatedly cited this lead, saying the U.S. is "leading China" in AI. But the gap may be narrowing as China's rapid advances, particularly following the emergence of Chinese AI firms such as DeepSeek, have raised concerns among U.S. policymakers and industry leaders. China is producing competitive AI models, expanding domestic chip development and investing heavily in AI research and deployment. A growing share of top AI researchers are now based in China, and Chinese companies have become major players in generative AI, robotics and industrial applications. China's government has also made AI leadership a strategic national priority, with Chinese President Xi previously calling for a global AI governance framework while simultaneously encouraging domestic innovation and deployment. Texas Fight Over Data Centers The debate about data centers escalated during Texas' 2026 gubernatorial campaign. In September, outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott ordered a moratorium on data center approvals, barring the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) from issuing new permits while collecting additional operational data from tech companies. “Simply put, Texans must come first. Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water and complete the ERCOT [Electric Reliability Council of Texas] and TWDB [Texas Water Development Board] audits. Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects," Abbott said in a statement. The freeze marked a shift from earlier in Abbott's tenure, when he called Texas “the epicenter of AI development,” adding: “We must ensure that America remains at the forefront of the AI revolution, and Texas is the place where that can happen.” Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa repeatedly criticized the industry's rapid expansion during her campaign, arguing the state lacked adequate oversight. At a campaign event in Amarillo, she described the boom as "the wild west of data centers." "They are owned by the richest men in the world. We're all footing the bill. There are no rules. It is the wild west of data centers," she said. Hinojosa pledged in an October video posted on X to maintain a statewide halt on new projects until lawmakers enact stricter regulations. "When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the Legislature to protect Texans," she said. Earlier this month on Fox News, the governor-elect elaborated on her proposal, stating that economic development and stronger regulations could coexist. "I don't hate data centers. I hate the way they're taking advantage of Texans. We don't have laws to protect Texans. We need a ban on new data center permits until we can pass laws to protect Texans and most importantly, and so Texans can have a seat at the table to decide if and how data centers come into their communities." Earlier this month, the governor notified TCEQ that it could resume reviewing and issuing data center permits after ERCOT had finished gathering information on potential community impacts for its audit report, according to the Houston Chronicle. The decision cleared the way for several major developments, including permits tied to SpaceX's proposed supercomputing facility and gas-fired power plant near Boca Chica, a CloudBurst project near San Marcos and an Atlas Energy Solutions project near Abilene. Water Supply Concerns Cruz's remarks come as researchers and environmental advocates warn that water demand tied to data center growth poses a significant planning challenge for the state. In a January report examining the potential impact of AI development on Texas water supplies, HARC's President and CEO John Hall called for greater oversight. "Our analysis makes one fact unavoidable: When we talk about data centers, we must talk about water," he said in a statement announcing the findings. "We can either plan now with foresight and transparency, or we will be forced to react later with our backs to the wall." Dr. Margaret Cook, the center's vice president of water and community resilience and the report's lead author, said Texas lacks a system for evaluating water impacts comparable to its planning process for electricity demand. "Texas' water planning process has a structural blind spot," she said in the report announcement. "ERCOT has begun developing processes to manage large load interconnections for energy, but no parallel process exists for water planning. This leaves utilities and city managers to negotiate individually with multinational technology firms, often without the data or leverage necessary to protect local resources and residents." The Greater Edwards Aquifer Alliance has also raised alarms. Speaking to Texas Public Radio in April, then-policy director Rachel Hanes said proposed AI data centers could have "very large impacts on our water supplies, on our energy supplies and public health, our coffers, our local government regulations and authorities and budgets." Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Jennifer Radcliffe and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: The Texas Republican claimed China-backed influence operations have helped rapidly shift public opinion against data centers.
