news.title: Son of Hamas chief survives Israeli air strike
news.text: The son of Hamas chief Khalil al-Hayya has survived an assassination attempt by the Israeli military, senior Hamas official Basem Naim says. He told Reuters Izzeldeen ‌al-Hayya and his family had survived a dawn air strike and Hamas sources said several people, including Hayya's daughter-in-law, had been wounded but there had been ‌no deaths. The Israeli military had no immediate comment. Naim described Izzeldeen al-Hayya, born in 1997, as the Hamas chief's last surviving son, with ‌four others having been killed by Israeli forces. The family of one of the late sons survived Friday's strike, Naim said. Hamas said in a statement the Israeli military had targeted a residential apartment, and linked the attack to threats Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has made against Hayya. Hamas accused Israel of seeking to undermine a 2025 Gaza ceasefire agreement and said Israel bore full responsibility for the consequences ‌of its continued attacks. ‌Izzeldeen is the ⁠twin brother of Hamam Khalil al-Hayya, who was killed in a 2025 Israeli air strike targeting ​Hamas leaders in Qatar, Naim said. Named Hamas' overall leader in July, Hayya narrowly escaped assassination himself in the Qatar strike. Two separate Israeli strikes killed five Palestinians in Gaza on Friday, medics said. The first strike killed three Palestinians and wounded two in the city of Rafah, medical sources told Reuters. The Israeli military ⁠spokesperson said the military had struck three militants without giving further information. ‌In the second ​attack, Palestinian medics said the two people, who worked as civil guards at an office of the Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) in Gaza City, ​were killed. ‌The MSF confirmed the two men were watchmen at the organisation, calling for accountability over the attack. It said the total ​number of its workers killed in Gaza reached 17. The Israeli military acknowledged ​the two men worked for MSF, describing them as Hamas militants who were "posing as humanitarian workers." Israel has continued to carry out attacks it says target Hamas but the attacks have also killed many civilians. The broader ceasefire plan, backed by US President Donald Trump, has not halted ​the ​violence or secured Hamas' disarmament. At least 1600 Palestinians ​and five Israeli soldiers have been killed since the ceasefire was ‌agreed in October 2025, according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies. Israeli troops control around two-thirds of Gaza, up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire, while Hamas controls a thin piece of territory along Gaza's coast. Israel's assault on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since 2023, caused a hunger crisis, internally displaced Gaza's entire population and led to assessments of genocide from scholars and a ​United Nations inquiry. news.title: Elon Musk’s SpaceX Giveaway Is a Lesson in Capitalism
news.text:
I will be donating another share of SpaceX to all kids in America every year— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 26, 2026

For those unfamiliar with Trump Accounts, they are tax-advantaged investment accounts established under President Donald Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act to help American children accumulate wealth from an early age. American children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, are also eligible for an initial $1,000 contribution from the federal government.

Based on SpaceX's stock price on November 25 and the approximately 72 million children living in the United States, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, the initial pledge could be worth approximately $18 billion if every child receives two shares, although the actual value will depend on the number of recipients, the company's stock price, and other factors.

Gwynne Shotwell, the company's president and chief operating officer, has also separately pledged more than two million SpaceX shares.

If SpaceX continues to grow and accomplish its ambitious technological objectives over the next several decades, millions of American children could potentially financially benefit from that progress. For children growing up in households with little to no investment wealth, this will also serve as an introduction to investing, an introduction to financial literacy, and an example of the long-term benefits of participating in the American economy.

This is such great news, and I think there is a much greater lesson to be learned from such remarkable actions. The very fact that Elon Musk is in a financial position to make such an extraordinary donation is a testament to the power of capitalism. This was only possible in an economic model that rewards hard work and good ideas. His wealth is largely the product of his ownership in companies that have developed products and services that millions of people around the world find valuable. Unfortunately, in America, this is becoming harder because of unnecessary rules and regulations. 

Incentive is the engine of a free-market economy. The idea of obtaining extraordinary financial rewards encourages individuals to undertake extraordinary risks, pursue ambitious and well-thought-out ideas, and develop technologies that might otherwise never exist. From revolutionizing the electric vehicle industry through Tesla to developing reusable rockets like SpaceX's Falcon 9 and providing high-speed satellite internet to remote parts of the world through Starlink, Musk and his people working at his companies have made extraordinary contributions to humanity and human progress.

Meanwhile, politicians like Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) have spent much of their political careers whining about how to tax and redistribute the wealth that other people have created. For example, Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) introduced legislation that would impose a 5% annual wealth tax on American billionaires. 

Related: Bernie Sanders Is a Millionaire, but Apparently Being a Billionaire Is Greed

What I find frustrating about much of the rhetoric surrounding socialist ideas is its emphasis on wealth redistribution rather than wealth creation. It does not ask “how can we make it easier for people to create wealth?” Instead, it asks, “How can we take from other people and punish those who are successful?” They are always discussing taking, but never building or creating. 

At some point, I think this obsession with economic inequality becomes a form of jealousy disguised as some form of moral superiority. A form of moral superiority that aims to flatten the socioeconomic gap by taking from others. 

It really reminds me of the fantastic speech Secretary of State Marco Rubio made while speaking about radical left-wing political violence earlier this year, describing the underlying resentment as:

It is a poisonous resentment cloaked in the language of equality and justice and liberation, an overwhelming need to tear down what greater men have built, to wreck what is beautiful and what is right on behalf of people who are only filled with ugliness and have nothing else to offer the world.

There is a major difference between wanting poor people to become richer and wanting rich people to become poorer. The former is motivated by a desire for prosperity and goodwill, while the latter is motivated by resentment and envy (which is also known to be a deadly sin in the Christian faith).

Rather than obsessing over how we can take away from the wealth of Elon Musk and other billionaires, we should be asking ourselves how we can create an economic environment that produces more people like Elon. Unfortunately, here in America, we have been shifting too far toward socialist economics and away from creating more wonderful people like Elon. 

America's future prosperity will depend not on how we can best redistribute the wealth of yesterday, but on how successfully we encourage the creation of the wealth of tomorrow.

news.title: US shoppers confront uphill battle in Black Friday discount quest
news.text:
People walk past stores offering Black Friday deals on 34th Street in New York City. (EPA Images pic)
LOS ANGELES: Inflation-weary US shoppers thronged malls and websites on Black Friday, the traditional kickoff to the holiday spending season, but many said they were struggling to find robust enough bargains to counter the pinch of high gas and grocery prices.
Spending is seen topping last year's strong figures by 4%-6%, forecasts show, but beneath top-line forecasts lie signs of stress.
Most of the gains will be attributable to inflation - which at 3.8% is about a percentage point higher than in each of the last two years - and consumer sentiment remains shaky.
Jasmine Peters, 37, went to the Westfield Century City mall in Los Angeles on Friday hoping to find steeper discounts in-store than online, but they didn't materialize, and by late morning, she was planning to leave the mall empty-handed.
Chris Nile, 30, was hoping for more than the US$50 discount he saw on a Nintendo Switch 2 gaming console, which brought the price to US$450. "Inflation is higher - hell, even the (McDonald's) McChicken is up," said Nile as he shopped for his two boys at the Crabtree Valley Mall in Raleigh, North Carolina.
Observers said consumers seemed less impressed by discounts, with stores needing to do more to draw them in. Target Corp, for example, gave away US$100 gift cards to the first 100 people in line at each store - with one lucky recipient receiving a US$1,000 card.
"Traffic levels in general seemed off compared to past holidays and seemed to lose steam early," said Michael Brown, Americas retail leader at consulting firm Kearney, who visited several stores in Westchester County, New York, on Friday morning.
US store visits were tracking 2% behind last year's as of late afternoon, at 530 million a little after 3:30 pm US eastern time, according to Passby, a geospatial analytics company that measures real-time foot traffic.
A November survey by the National Retail Federation found that 82% of consumers are taking steps to manage holiday costs this year, like buying less expensive gifts. Nile - like many US shoppers - said he chose to bargain-hunt in person, in part to avoid shipping costs.
AI could also scramble the year's shopping dynamics. As consumers use it to find bargains or even complete purchases — and retailers become increasingly adept at altering prices — the deepest discounts could come closer to Christmas.
Online spending on Black Friday itself, though, was expected to jump 9.2% from a year ago to US$12.9 billion, according to a forecast from Adobe Analytics, the arm of Adobe that analyzes customer behavior.
Measured growth
Economic worries aside, top-line spending is expected to be robust.
Thanksgiving Day saw consumers spend US$7.1 billion online, according to Adobe, a 10.4% jump over last year, fueled by big discounts on electronics, toys and apparel. Indeed, store visits to electronics retailer Best Buy were tracking 4.4% higher than last Black Friday at midday, according to Passby. Visits to Walmart and Target were flat to slightly up.
Overall, the National Retail Federation sees November-December holiday retail sales rising 4.2% year-over-year, to just above $1 trillion.
High living costs emerged as a key issue earlier this month when voters handed Democrats sweeping electoral victories, punishing US President Donald Trump for an Iran war that's pushed the cost of living higher.
Even higher earners may be stretched.
Holiday spending forecasts mostly predated the recent stock market correction that followed the midterms, turmoil at chipmaker Nvidia, and mounting concerns around an AI bubble. The decline could dampen the wealth effect that has seen affluent shoppers splurge, UBS analysts said in a note on Tuesday.
Embattled toys
Higher input costs, particularly from oil derivatives like plastic, are hitting some products more than others.
Prices of toys — generally high in plastic — have risen 13.2% since the start of the year, pushing Barbie maker Mattel this month to cut its annual forecast as consumers balked at higher costs.
But some unlikely products are buoying the toy category. Best Buy and Target have both flagged trading cards — including Pokemon and Magic: The Gathering products — as a key growth driver. Squishy NeeDoh toys are also in hot demand, according to e-commerce marketing platform Omnisend.
Lego also appeared to be in high demand, with the Passby figures showing its stores' foot traffic up more than 5% in mid-afternoon versus the same time of day last Black Friday. It wasn't necessarily kids driving the growth - most of those online were adults, part of the "kidult" craze that has swept the toy industry in recent years.
Jaime Oquendo, 46, was the first to enter the Lego store at the Westfield Century City mall in Los Angeles when it opened, to buy a new Godzilla set, released on Black Friday at US$450.
“I actually made sure I had money set aside all year, back when they announced it, just to make sure I could get my hands on one,” Oquendo said.
news.summary: Black Friday spending is forecast to exceed last year's strong figures by 4%-6%, despite underlying signs of financial strain.
news.author: Reuters

news.title: U.S. Disables Ship Attempting to Breach Iran Blockade — Tehran Threatens Military Action from ‘Air and Sea’
news.text:
U.S. forces struck and disabled a commercial vessel attempting to breach the naval blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced Friday, as Tehran threatened military action from “the air and sea.”

The strike comes as the Trump administration intensifies its campaign to cut off the Islamic Republic’s remaining sources of revenue, while Iranian officials vow to break the American blockade and maintain what they claim is their closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

A U.S. military aircraft struck the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman Thursday after the bulk carrier departed the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas and attempted to evade the blockade despite multiple warnings, CENTCOM said.

The strike disabled the ship’s propulsion system, leaving its civilian crew unharmed.

“CENTCOM continues to strictly enforce the blockade,” the command said, noting that U.S. forces have redirected 158 commercial vessels and disabled six that refused to comply.

Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Aerospace Force Commander Majid Mousavi warned Friday that Iran’s enemies should expect military action from “the air and sea,” vowing to break the U.S. blockade.

“No blockade will withstand Iran’s national will and defence capabilities,” Mousavi wrote on X. “Breaking the blockade is a mission and a firm resolve.”

Iranian Navy Commander Adm. Shahram Irani claimed operations to break the blockade were already underway, saying Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had lifted geographical restrictions on Iran’s military operations.

Speaking on Iranian state television, Irani claimed U.S. forces were now “begging” for passage through the Strait of Hormuz and vowed to drive them back to the Bay of Pigs in Cuba, “where they belong.”

“We have a free hand to carry out the assigned missions,” he said

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi had declared the blockade an “act of war” last Saturday, vowing that Tehran would take whatever measures necessary to break it.

President Donald Trump dared Tehran to challenge the blockade Sunday, warning, “I hope they do; they’ll all be at the bottom of the sea like the rest of the navy.”

The president touted the effectiveness of the blockade during a Thanksgiving call Thursday, praising sailors aboard the USS Portland for their role in enforcing what he described as “the most successful blockade in naval history.”

“Not one ship has gotten through to Iran,” Trump said.

While Trump has signaled that he is inclined to hold off on another major military offensive against Iran until after the start of the new year, his administration has continued to escalate its economic campaign against the Islamic Republic.

The Treasury Department unveiled sweeping new sanctions Monday targeting Iran’s shadow banking networks, which Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described as “the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime.”

Bessent revealed Wednesday that Iran had exhausted its remaining supplies of oil available for sale at sea.

“The Iranian regime is a sinking ship,” he wrote. “After failing to load a single tanker since Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast in August, Iran doesn’t have a drop of oil on the water left to sell.”

Beyond restricting Iran’s maritime trade, Washington has moved to shut down alternative routes Tehran uses to circumvent sanctions, with CENTCOM announcing Task Force Iron Gate earlier this month to target illicit shipments through overland corridors and the Caspian Sea.

Following reports that Washington had pressed Baghdad to shut down routes used to disguise Iranian crude as Iraqi oil, Trump voiced support Friday for Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq and “stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil.”

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian himself acknowledged the severity of the economic pressure last Saturday, describing it as a “silent war” that was “far more difficult than one in which missiles are launched and destruction is caused.”

Iranian authorities have been forced to ration electricity and scale back food subsidies amid mounting economic hardship, while a truckers’ strike triggered by rising fuel costs and rampant inflation entered its sixth day Friday.

Despite the economic toll, Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, insisted Friday that Tehran would not allow the U.S. naval blockade to remain in place, while maintaining Iran’s claim that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed.
news.summary:
U.S. forces struck and disabled a commercial vessel attempting to breach the naval blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced Friday, as Tehran threatened military action from “the air and sea.”
